prize_parts.citation: for showing, with credible empirical designs, how import competition and technological change reshape labour demand, wage inequality and the adjustment of workers and local labour markets

statement.case_for: My configuration has changed in one respect. I keep B023 as my single preferred achievement, but the third name moves from Katz to Dorn, and the citation is anchored in the empirical analysis of shocks to labour demand and local adjustment. In round 1 I called Dorn's omission the main weakness of my proposal and said I would welcome a swap. The exchange gave me three reasons to make it. First, the Autor-Dorn-Hanson papers are the jointly authored core of the import-competition evidence, with a common design and data, so crediting them is the sharpest attribution available for this ballot. Second, as I recall, Dorn also co-authored with Autor on job polarisation and the growth of low-skill service jobs. That means the trio can still cover the technology strand without crediting the older skill-premium literature, where Katz shares credit with Goldin, Murphy and others outside the credited names. Third, Dreber, Boppart and Stromberg each pressed the bundling and attribution point from different directions, and I find it substantive. This is not a change in my assessment of the science. The designs (quasi-experimental variation, administrative and local-market data) raised credibility standards in applied economics, and the main findings have survived one to three decades of replication and criticism. Local adjustment to trade shocks is slow and costly, which contradicted the expectation of rapid reallocation. That finding has had large influence on trade, labour and public economics and on the policy debate on globalisation and automation. I do not treat the ballot's breadth of ranking across members as evidence of merit.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged in kind. B023 joins a technology-and-wage-structure line with a trade-shock line, and any three names leave out someone with a real claim. With Dorn in place of Katz, the citation no longer credits the long-run skill-biased technical change evidence, and the task-model theory sits partly with Acemoglu and Restrepo, who are outside the credited names. The citation therefore has to claim the empirical analysis of labour demand and local adjustment, not the task-model theory. The magnitude and persistence of the local trade-shock effects, and the shift-share inference behind them, are still debated. I judge that debate to bear more on the size of the estimates than on the core qualitative finding, but that is a judgement from recall and not a source check. On the chair's question about B006, a two-name Kiyotaki-Moore prize would be the cleanest attribution on the shortlist, and I would not oppose it. It would not move ahead of B023 for me on a single criterion. That criterion is the weight of direct empirical evidence: how far a discovery's central claim has been tested and re-tested against data. Collateral-channel identification is conceded by several B006 supporters to be mixed, whereas the local-labour-market evidence has been scrutinised repeatedly. The margin is narrow, and I would regard B006 as the strongest alternative. B047 has a similarly clean core in Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes, with its own acknowledged cost in the omission of Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin.

responses.point: Dreber proposes Autor, Hanson and Dorn and says the Autor-Dorn-Hanson papers are the unified, jointly authored core, with the same design and data. She argues that Katz's skill-premium work overlaps with the Goldin-Katz tradition and that Katz's mobility work belongs to a different ballot (B031). She would widen the citation's wording and not drop Dorn if the technology strand is to be explicit.
responses.response: She moved me. I had weighted Katz because the wage-structure evidence is the foundation on which the trade-shock work builds. But a citation can name that foundation without crediting its originators, whereas a prize that omits a co-originator of the central papers has a visible defect. I also accept her suggestion to anchor the citation in the empirical evidence on labour demand and local adjustment and not claim the task-model theory. Where I differ slightly is on the Goldin overlap. As I recall, the 2023 prize recognised women's labour-market outcomes, so I would not treat that overlap as decisive. It is one reason among several, and I rely on recall for it.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B023 first with Autor, Hanson and Katz. He argues that Katz anchors the long-run technology and wages evidence and that Autor spans both strands. He says he would not object to Dorn instead of Katz if the Committee prefers the narrower citation, and that Dorn is arguably equally deserving. He names B006 as the stronger-attributed alternative if B023's attribution cannot be settled.
responses.response: We now agree that the third name is an open attribution choice, and I have settled it differently from his lean. His point that Autor spans both strands is what makes the Dorn version defensible for me. The Autor-Dorn work on polarisation, as I recall it, carries the technology side without requiring Katz. I also take his B006 fallback seriously. The test that keeps B023 ahead for me is whether attribution can be made clean. With Autor, Dorn and Hanson it can, because the paper trail points to three people. If the Committee judges that the technology and trade strands cannot share one citation, B006 as a Kiyotaki-Moore pair is where I would look next, not a diluted B023.

responses.point: Hassler's current round-1 file prefers a three-name B006 (Kiyotaki, Moore and Gertler). He ties Gertler's credit to the intermediary-frictions work with Kiyotaki and the quantitative financial-friction models, not to the accelerator papers that overlap Bernanke's 2022 prize. He says the Committee should state openly that the accelerator credit is partly absorbed.
responses.response: I am responding to his three-name file, not the two-name proposal I answered in round 1. His distinction is coherent, and a citation worded around collateral constraints and balance-sheet frictions would avoid re-recognising the accelerator. I cannot judge from the evidence supplied whether the intermediary-frictions papers are separable enough in credit, and that is the question I would put to the B006 supporters. My difficulty is not attribution, since the Kiyotaki-Moore core is not disputed. It is the evidentiary base. His own file concedes that identification of the collateral channel is mixed and that the evidence is more convincing for amplification in general than for the specific mechanism. For that reason I rank B006 as my first alternative and not first. I would accept the two-name version as a fallback for the same reason he would.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B047 first and B023 third. He argues that the China-shock papers belong to Autor, Dorn and Hanson and the task and skill-bias work involves Katz and others outside the credited names, so a bundle that merges two discoveries and omits Dorn is harder to defend than a single method with a clear core. His own B023 variant is Autor and Hanson only.
responses.response: His critique of my round-1 trio is largely right, and the Dorn swap answers it in part. I still disagree with the two-name cut. Dorn is a full co-author of the central papers, so dropping him to shrink the number would create an attribution defect where none needs to exist, given that the cap of three does not bind here. I also take his comparison with B047 seriously. The Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes trio is a clean method with a long applied record. I rank it as an alternative on those grounds. I put B023 ahead on the nature of the evidence. The B023 evidence is a set of research designs that have been repeatedly re-examined, with identifying variation that is transparent. BLP's counterfactuals depend more heavily on functional-form and equilibrium assumptions, which he himself lists. That is a difference in weighting, not a claim that B047 is weak.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee reads technology and trade shocks as one achievement about labour demand, or as two that should not share a citation. My answer depends on the citation staying anchored in the empirical analysis of labour demand and local adjustment.
Whether Dorn's role in the technology and polarisation strand is as substantial as I recall. I rely on recall of the authorship and have not verified contribution or citation data.

How large and persistent the local effects of import competition are, and how robust the shift-share inference is. I judge that the core qualitative finding has survived, but I cannot check this from the supplied evidence.
How much thematic overlap with the 2021, 2023 and 2024 prizes should count against B023. I would want the Committee to apply the same standard to B006's proximity to the 2022 prize.
Whether B006, as a two-name or three-name award, would be preferred to B023 once the empirical status of the collateral channel is weighed. The margin is narrow.
statement.conflict_note: Updated for round 2. My preferred configuration is now Autor, Hanson and Dorn. My profile lists no co-authorship or institutional tie to any of them, and Katz is no longer in my configuration. My own field of empirical labour economics and policy evaluation is close to B023, and as chair in 2021 I praised natural experiments publicly, which could predispose me to this style of evidence. I have tried to apply the common criteria and have weighed B006 and B047 on the same standards. I overlapped institutionally with Hassler and Krusell at Stockholm University (2010-17), which is not a co-authorship. I share a co-author, Bertil Holmlund, with Hjalmarsson, which is not a direct tie. None of the credited names on B006 or B047 appears among my listed co-authors. Disclosed, not adjudicated.
